issues.legal_issue: A landlord seeking expedited recovery on the basis of a claimed personal or dependent’s need must establish a genuine requirement, although that requirement is presumed genuine unless the tenant rebuts the presumption with cogent material.
material_facts: The landlord sought recovery of rented premises for personal use or use by a dependent ordinarily living with the landlord.
The tenant challenged the asserted need, but in some applications offered only bare assertions or allegations about other property without sufficient supporting particulars or evidence.
The statutory scheme restricts the landlord’s use and transfer of premises recovered through this procedure and imposes consequences for breach.
issues.conclusion: The landlord’s pleaded need is presumed genuine and bona fide, but the tenant may rebut that presumption with strong, cogent material; a mere assertion is insufficient.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 13-B, 18-A(4) and 18-A(5) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, the tenant may seek leave to contest by affidavit disclosing facts that would disentitle the landlord from recovery. The restrictions and safeguards in Sections 13-B(3) and 19(2-B) support a strong presumption of genuine need, which remains rebuttable. Genuine need is more than a wish or pretext: Ram Dass v. Ishwar Chander; Bega Begum v. Abdul Ahad Khan; Surjit Singh Kalra v. Union of India; Shiv Sarup Gupta v. Dr. Mahesh Chand Gupta. Statutory language is to be read according to its plain meaning and in a way that advances the enactment’s purpose: K.P. Verghese v. Income Tax Officer; Babaji Kondaji Garad v. Nasik Merchants Co-operative Bank; Ravulu Subba Rao v. Commissioner of Income-Tax.

predicates.landlord_claims_personal_or_dependent_us: The landlord claims that the premises are required for the landlord’s use or for a dependent ordinarily living with the landlord.
predicates.statutory_recovery_restrictions_apply: The landlord is subject to restrictions on dealing with the recovered premises and consequences for breaching those restrictions.

issues.definition: When a specially classified landlord seeks the premises for personal or dependent use under a regime that restricts the landlord’s conduct after recovery, the need is treated as genuine unless the tenant rebuts it with cogent material.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant is entitled to leave to contest an expedited recovery application when the tenant’s affidavit discloses material facts that, if established, could defeat one of the landlord’s required grounds for recovery.
material_facts: The tenants were required to seek leave to contest by affidavit.
Some tenants challenged the landlord’s status, ownership, return to the country, duration of ownership, or genuineness of need.

The court held that bare assertions, unsupported allegations about other properties, or grounds outside the statutory requirements did not suffice; material, particularized evidence could warrant leave.
issues.conclusion: The tenant’s defence is confined to the statutory grounds for recovery, and leave is warranted only where the affidavit presents a strong, material challenge to a ground the landlord must establish.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 18-A(4) and 18-A(5) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 require the tenant to disclose in an affidavit facts that would disentitle the landlord from recovery under Section 13-B. The inquiry is confined to the matters the landlord must establish under Section 13-B, including qualifying status, return, ownership for the required duration, and genuine need. A bare assertion does not rebut the presumption of genuine need; the tenant must provide necessary facts and particulars, supported by documentary evidence where available.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord who is of Indian origin and has settled outside the country for an uncertain period may use the special recovery procedure after returning, without proving an intention to settle permanently in the country.
material_facts: The landlords in the appeals had settled abroad for employment, business, or other purposes and sought recovery after returning to the country.
Tenants argued that the landlords had not returned permanently or did not intend to settle permanently.
The statutory definition included persons of Indian origin settled permanently or temporarily abroad in circumstances indicating a stay abroad for an uncertain period.
issues.conclusion: Permanent return or permanent resettlement is not required; a qualifying landlord may return temporarily and seek possession for the landlord’s or a dependent’s use.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(dd) and 13-B of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 must be read together. A person of Indian origin who has settled abroad for employment, business, or another purpose indicating an intention to stay abroad for an uncertain period may qualify, and the words requiring return do not require permanent resettlement. A temporary stay abroad for a defined course or degree, by contrast, does not by itself indicate an uncertain period of stay.

issues.legal_issue: A specially classified landlord may seek recovery of premises of one use category for a requirement involving a different use category.
material_facts: A tenant occupied a non-residential premises while the landlord sought it for residential use.
The tenant argued that a non-residential premises could not be recovered for residential purposes.
The statutory provision allowed recovery of residential, scheduled, or non-residential premises when required for the landlord’s or a dependent’s use.
issues.conclusion: The difference between the premises’ category and the landlord’s intended use does not by itself bar recovery.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13-B of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 permits recovery of residential, scheduled, or non-residential premises for the landlord’s or a dependent’s use; it does not require the intended use to match the category of the premises.

issues.legal_issue: A qualifying landlord need not personally present the recovery application if it is filed through an attorney and the landlord later comes to the country.
material_facts: A landlord’s recovery application was filed through an attorney.
The landlord later came to the country.
The tenant challenged the application on the basis that the landlord had not personally come to file it.
issues.conclusion: Filing through an attorney is not a bar when the landlord later comes to the country.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13-B of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 does not require a qualifying landlord personally to file the application in the country; filing through an attorney satisfies the requirement where the landlord later comes to the country.

predicates.landlord_later_returns_to_country: The landlord comes to the country after the application is filed.

issues.definition: An application filed through an attorney is not barred when the qualifying landlord later comes to the country.

issues.legal_issue: Earlier proceedings under general rent-recovery provisions do not by themselves bar a later application under the special recovery procedure.
material_facts: A landlord had previously pursued ejectment proceedings under the general provisions of the rent law.
The landlord later sought recovery under the special procedure for the specially classified landlord category.
The tenant argued that the earlier proceedings barred the later application.
issues.conclusion: The earlier proceedings do not bar an application under the special procedure.
issues.legal_principle: The special procedure under Section 13-B of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 is distinct from proceedings under the general provisions, and earlier general proceedings do not by themselves prevent use of the special procedure.

predicates.earlier_general_eviction_proceeding_exis: The landlord previously pursued recovery of the premises under general rent-recovery grounds.

issues.definition: A prior general recovery proceeding does not, by itself, prevent a landlord from bringing a later application under the special recovery procedure.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord may recover premises to adapt or reconstruct them to meet the landlord’s requirements, provided the landlord complies with the restrictions governing use and transfer after recovery.
material_facts: A landlord sought recovery in order to use the premises for a business and later reconstruct the building according to the landlord’s needs.
The tenant argued that reconstruction was not an available ground for recovery.
The court found no prohibition on reconstruction so long as the landlord did not breach the applicable post-recovery conditions.
issues.conclusion: Reconstruction according to the landlord’s needs is not prohibited, provided the landlord complies with the applicable restrictions after recovery.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13-B of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 requires the landlord to establish a genuine need for the premises but does not prohibit adapting or reconstructing them to meet that need. The landlord remains subject to the restrictions in Section 13-B(3) and the consequences under Section 19(2-B).
